Interviewer: Welcome. This is a mock backend engineering interview. We are interested in how you identify assumptions and tradeoffs. Please distinguish a guarantee from a common implementation detail, and say when you need more requirements.
Interviewer: Our team operates a small web service used by internal engineering teams. It stores documents and schedules background indexing jobs. Some clients run on unreliable networks. The service has several replicas, a relational database, a shared cache, and a queue of background work. We deploy changes gradually and want to preserve compatibility with old clients during a rollout.
Interviewer: Earlier we discussed observability. We collect request counts, errors, latency histograms and queue age, with trace identifiers across services. We do not log request credentials. Averages alone can hide tail latency. When a user reports a slow operation, I would ask you to identify where time is spent before proposing an optimization.
Interviewer: Consider the difference between waiting time and processing time. A healthy worker may still receive work too late if the producer outruns the consumers. Increasing concurrency can increase contention, memory use and failure rates. We want a bounded policy that makes overload visible and preserves work that must be durable.
Interviewer: Another topic we covered was schema changes. A database migration and an application rollout do not happen atomically. Old application versions may continue to read and write while new ones are deployed. We would discuss an expand-and-contract approach, compatibility tests, a backfill, and when removing an old field becomes safe. These were earlier topics, not the question I am asking now.
Interviewer: For code explanations, please describe the data structures, time and space complexity, and important edge cases. Distinguish expected hash-table complexity from a worst-case bound. If object identity matters, say so rather than comparing payload values. You can use Java, C++, Python or pseudocode when the current question does not specify a language.
Interviewer: We also talked about caching. A cache can reduce repeated reads but does not automatically become the durable source of truth. Invalidation and freshness depend on the product requirements. If a downstream system fails, think about what can be retried safely and how uncertain outcomes are reconciled. Do not infer that every operation is idempotent.
Interviewer: Our examples are deliberately small enough to discuss without a whiteboard. We may change one constraint after your first answer. When that happens, revise the current approach and explain which assumption changed. If I repeat an unchanged question, you do not need to create a separate discussion. If I explicitly return to a topic after another question, that is a genuine revisit.
Interviewer: Only my playback is being transcribed here; the candidate's microphone is excluded. A later question referring to the candidate's spoken answer cannot be assessed from this transcript. A useful response can acknowledge the gap and explain what a strong answer would contain, without inventing a quote or claiming the candidate was correct.
Interviewer: To close the earlier discussion, we considered operational recovery. After a process restart, durable records should explain what completed and what needs reconciliation. A successful acknowledgment from one component does not prove that a separate external action committed. We would use documented guarantees and tests around failure boundaries, rather than assume everything runs exactly once.
Interviewer: We are moving to a fresh technical question now. Earlier examples are context about the interview style; they do not impose extra language versions, data structure restrictions, or durability requirements on this new question. Please answer the current wording and any explicit correction to it. Keep the hint concise while retaining every requested part.
